html:
A suspension bridge over the Danube in Budapest, opened in 1849, the first permanent bridge across the river in the city. It joined the towns of Buda and Pest.

Before it, the crossing was a bridge of boats taken down in winter, when people had to walk on the ice or wait. Count István Széchenyi, a reformer who wanted to modernise Hungary, pushed for a fixed bridge after he was once stuck on the wrong side for days. The English engineer William Tierney Clark designed it, and the Scot Adam Clark led the building. Széchenyi insisted that nobles pay the toll like everyone else, a break with old privilege.

It was nearly finished during the revolution of 1848 and 1849 and opened in November 1849. It helped make one city of Buda and Pest, which were united in 1873. Retreating German troops blew it up in January 1945. It was rebuilt and reopened in 1949, a hundred years after the first opening.
sum: A suspension bridge over the Danube in Budapest, opened in 1849, the first permanent bridge across the river in the city. It joined the towns of Buda and Pest.
